# Published hard-to-round inputs for atan, one double per line as its raw bits in hex
# (Double.doubleToRawLongBits), read by Inputs.hardCases("atan"). Lines starting with # are
# comments. Only the input values are taken from the source below; they are numeric facts.
#
# At such an input the exact atan(x) lies unusually close to a rounding boundary of binary64
# (a midpoint between two doubles for round-to-nearest, a double itself for the directed
# modes), so an implementation's last few rounding errors decide which double it returns. For a
# port that follows fdlibm's operations exactly they are no harder than any other input; their
# use here is that a dropped correction term or a reassociated sum, a change far below one ulp,
# is most likely to flip the result exactly at these points.
#
# Section 1: V. Lefevre, hard-to-round cases in round-to-nearest, file testlibm-data (updated
# 2020-11-27), https://www.vinc17.net/research/testlibm/testlibm-data.xz, from the page
# https://www.vinc17.net/research/testlibm/, which states no licence or reuse terms. Every
# line for "atn" in mode N, in the file's order, written by dev/testlibm-extract.py (python3 -I
# dev/testlibm-extract.py atn atan testlibm-data.xz), which derives atan(x) itself (a Taylor
# series after halving the angle, pi from Machin's formula) and rechecks each line with
# 400-digit decimal arithmetic before printing it: every input is a double, the file's result
# is atan(x) rounded to nearest, and the file's direction bit is the 54th bit of the exact
# atan(x). The recheck is also what shows the tag "atn" is atan's. Measured by the same run: of
# these 1735 inputs all have at least 45 bits after the round bit pointing at the midpoint (the
# exact result within 2^-45 ulp of it). All are positive: atan is odd, and the tests also draw
# the negated inputs.
